actors.name: Republic of Arkania
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.

actors.name: Cestia
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.

cons.reason: The claimed "consolidated, stable final settlement" is not genuinely consolidated or stable. Arkania retains unilateral scheduling and fee authority and treats both the scheduled review mechanism and the consultation channel as advisory only. That leaves Cestia's trading partners—including Belvar's partners—subject to unilateral tolls with no genuine recourse, which is precisely the source of the ongoing friction. Cestia itself continues to press Arkania to soften or remove fees and to make decision-making genuinely multilateral, so the regime remains contested rather than settled. A settlement that is advisory-only and unilateral cannot deliver the durable stability the effect claims; it risks renewed escalation if the Strait's commercial users are denied genuine voice, and it does not resolve the underlying dispute that brought Belvar's task group to the Strait in the first place.

Endorsing the Arkanian charter formalizes Arkanian scheduling lead over the Strait, which is precisely the unilateral authority that threatens Cestia's grain trade and regional stability. The consultative seat is non-binding and Arkania retains the power to set fees on non-Arkanian shipping, so Cestia's toll-free passage is not durable—Arkania can revise terms once the charter is locked in. Formalizing the charter also isolates Belvar and raises escalation risk to the very shipping Cestia depends on, so the desired effect of a secure, stable grain route is not actually achieved.

Cestia's desired effect would require Arkania to relinquish unilateral scheduling authority and remove transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping — the two core deliverables Arkania's domestic nationalists demand and the very substance of the Strait Transit Authority charter that Cestia itself formally endorsed. The review mechanism Arkania formalised was designed to keep fees transparent, modest and predictable, not to abolish them or to convert scheduling to genuine multilateral decision-making; Cestia's three conditions (toll-free Cestian passage, permanent consultative seat, no foreign military presence) are already honoured in full, so this ask goes beyond anything Cestia committed to. Moving to genuine multilateral scheduling would also undermine the Arkanian-led authority Cestia endorsed and could destabilise the stable, non-confrontational arrangement that has kept the Strait open and Belvar's task group standing down without a foothold.

The desired effect rests on a false premise that Arkania's unilateral scheduling and transit fees are the root cause of escalation risk. In fact, Cestia has formally endorsed the Arkanian-led Strait Transit Authority with Arkania as scheduling lead and toll-free Cestian shipping, and Cestia's coalition will not tolerate any foreign military presence on its soil. Belvar's own mandate has already lapsed without confrontation and its domestic support for a prolonged deployment is weak, so the escalation pressure is already dissipating through the cooperative civilian channel Arkania opened. Restructuring the Authority into genuine three-state shared scheduling would require reopening an arrangement Cestia has already endorsed and would strip Arkania of the scheduling authority and fee revenue its domestic mandate requires, all without any demonstrated benefit to a Strait that is already open and commercially stable. The proposal is therefore not a genuine compromise but a means to preserve Belvar's task group and foothold ambitions, and it should not be conceded.

Belvar's desired effect hinges on securing a "durable non-basing foothold at a Cestian port." But Cestia's coalition is held together by a single promise: no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. A standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port—even if framed as "non-basing"—is a foreign military foothold on Cestian territory and would collapse the coalition, which is one of Cestia's core objectives. The argument's premise that this "respects Cestia's sovereignty red line" is therefore false, and this element of the desired effect is not achievable as proposed.

The desired effect depends on Cestia reversing its formal endorsement of the Arkanian-led Strait Transit Authority and on accepting a standing port-access arrangement at a Cestian port — both of which Cestia has already publicly rejected. Cestia's coalition has formally endorsed the charter on three conditions (toll-free Cestian shipping, a consultative scheduling seat, and no foreign military presence) and has explicitly rejected "any Belvar foothold or standing access arrangement at a Cestian port." The proposal's port-access element, even framed as non-basing, is precisely the standing arrangement Cestia's coalition will not tolerate, and its coalition government remains intact. With Cestia's endorsement locked in and the Authority already formalised, there is no coalition path for Cestia to abandon the charter, so the multilateral regime with shared scheduling and no unilateral tolls cannot be established as proposed.

The desired effect is unachievable as a package because it depends on a "non-basing port access arrangement at a Cestian port." Cestia has publicly and repeatedly rejected any standing access or foothold at a Cestian port, however framed, and such an arrangement would collapse Cestia's coalition government. Cestia will not consent to it, so this element cannot be established. The multilateral transit regime and no-unilateral-tolls elements are welcome and consistent with Cestia's interests, but the port-access element makes the proposal unacceptable in its current form and would fail to secure Cestia's cooperation.

Arkania's proposal assumes Cestia will commit to an Arkanian-led authority, but the transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping would raise costs for Cestia's grain customers and trading partners, directly threatening the export economy on which the coalition depends. Moreover, the stated aim of isolating Belvar risks provoking Belvar to escalate its naval presence or pressure, turning the Strait into a confrontation zone and disrupting the very shipping Cestia cannot afford to lose. Cestia has not agreed to these terms and will not be rushed into a commitment that could collapse its coalition or destabilise the Strait, so securing Cestia's support is far from assured.

The desired effect claims the Strait remains commercially stable and Belvar's escalation risk is reduced, but Arkania retains unilateral scheduling authority and transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping, including Cestia's trading partners. Arkania has already declined to soften the fee structure (turn 2), so the very grievance driving Cestia's and Belvar's objections is left unaddressed. A civilian consultation channel does not resolve the unilateral authority that is the root cause of the tension; it merely papers over it, so the claimed stability and reduced escalation risk are not credible and the underlying conflict persists.

First, a "durable non-basing foothold at a Cestian port" is still a foreign military presence on Cestian soil, which Cestia's governing coalition has an absolute red line against under any arrangement; Cestia has already signalled openness to a cooperative regime with Arkania precisely on the condition of no foreign soldiers. Belvar cannot secure a foothold Cestia will not grant. Second, Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment is weak, so any foothold would not "outlast the crisis" as claimed. Third, the "free of tolls" framing overreaches: Cestia requires toll-free passage only for its own flagged shipping, not a blanket abolition of transit fees, so Arkania can still fund its authority on non-Cestian, non-Arkanian traffic without violating Cestia's conditions. The negotiated regime Belvar proposes therefore neither secures its foothold nor denies Arkania its funding basis.

Cestia's request to use the review mechanism to soften or remove transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping conflicts directly with Arkania's core objective of funding the Authority through those fees, and the review mechanism is advisory only under the settled Arkanian-led charter that Cestia itself endorses. The fee schedule is already transparent, modest and predictable, and Cestia's three conditions (toll-free Cestian passage, permanent consultative seat, no foreign military presence) are honoured in practice. The Strait is open and commercially stable with low escalation risk; there is no demonstrated basis to restructure the fee schedule or dilute Arkanian scheduling authority, and doing so would undermine the Authority's funding base and the domestic mandate Arkania must deliver.

Cestia's desired effect is not achievable through the review mechanism and would undermine the very arrangement Cestia endorsed. The scheduled review was established as advisory only, and Arkania retains unilateral scheduling and fee authority under the charter Cestia itself ratified; genuine multilateral decision-making would require renegotiating that charter, not invoking its review clause. Removing transit fees on all non-Arkanian shipping would strip the Authority of its funding basis and contradict Arkania's domestic mandate, so Arkania will not implement it. Cestia's three conditions (toll-free Cestian passage, permanent consultative seat, no foreign military presence) are already fully honoured in practice, so the effect's stated stability and coalition goals are already met without fee removal; pressing beyond them into genuine multilateral scheduling would expose Cestia's limited leverage and risk destabilizing its own coalition. The Strait remains open and commercially stable under the existing regime, so the effect's core premise holds regardless of fee changes.

The proposed Authority grants Arkania unilateral scheduling authority and levies transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping, which will directly raise the cost and risk of the grain exports on which Cestia's coalition and economy depend. Cestia's endorsement is conditional and its coalition is fragile; a fee regime that hits the very trade Cestia lives on will erode that endorsement and could collapse the government Arkania claims to be protecting. The promised "civilian consultation channel" to Belvar is a fig leaf: it gives Belvar and other users no vote or veto over scheduling or fees, so it does not address the core objection to unilateral control and will not keep Belvar engaged—it will instead be read as a pretext to let Belvar's mandate lapse, provoking resistance and escalation rather than the peaceful resolution the argument claims. A regime that excludes the affected parties from real authority is not a stable settlement and will not secure the Strait's free and reliable transit.

Cestia's coalition will not accept Arkanian scheduling lead even with a consultative seat: the "permanent Cestian seat with consultative scheduling rights" grants Cestia no real authority while Arkania retains the lead and the power to levy fees on non-Arkanian shipping. Those fees raise costs for Cestia's grain customers and trading partners, directly threatening the exports Cestia's economy depends on, so Cestia has strong incentive to reject the charter rather than endorse it. Nor is Belvar reliably isolated: its task group is on station and it has publicly committed to keeping the Strait free, so Arkania cannot assume time simply favours it or that Belvar's weak domestic support guarantees inaction within its mandate.

The desired effect of exempting all of Cestia's trading partners from transit fees would gut the funding mechanism of the Strait Transit Authority that Cestia itself endorsed. The Authority's fees on non-Arkanian shipping are the agreed funding source for the scheduling regime; extending exemptions to every Cestian trading partner would make the Authority financially unviable and undermine the very charter Cestia endorsed. The three conditions (toll-free Cestian-flagged shipping, permanent consultative seat, no foreign military presence) are already honored in practice; the fee structure is a separate, agreed element of the charter, not one of the three conditions. Softening it to spare all of Cestia's partners would also undercut the domestic mandate Arkania needs to keep the Authority stable, risking the very escalation Cestia wants to avoid.

The desired effect of securing "Belvar's non-confrontational acceptance" and Cestia's continued endorsement while preserving Arkanian unilateral scheduling authority and transit fees is unlikely to hold, because the root cause of the tension is precisely that unilateral authority and the fees themselves. Arkania has repeatedly characterized the consultation channel as advisory only, so a "genuine consultative role" and a "civilian advisory role" give neither Cestia nor Belvar any binding voice over scheduling or fee-setting; the review mechanism is discretionary and leaves fees on Cestia's trading partners intact. Cestia's own turn-2 and turn-3 arguments pressed Arkania to soften the fee structure and avoid isolating Belvar, and Belvar has publicly committed to opposing any single power imposing unilateral transit authority or tolls. A modest, predictable fee with an advisory channel does not address that core objection, so it will not deliver the genuine acceptance the effect claims; it entrenches the very unilateral authority and fees that Cestia and Belvar oppose, leaving the underlying dispute unresolved and the Strait's stability hostage to Arkanian discretion.

The transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping would tax Cestia's trading partners and could raise the cost of moving grain through the Strait, directly threatening Cestia's core interest in uninterrupted, affordable exports. Even with a civilian consultation channel to Belvar, Arkanian unilateral scheduling authority backed by fees on others is likely to be read by Belvar as entrenchment rather than accommodation, risking the very escalation and Strait disruption Cestia cannot afford. This fee-and-lead structure may therefore fail to deliver the stable, non-confrontational outcome the effect claims and could erode the regional legitimacy it needs to succeed.

Cestia's desired effect would require Arkania to relinquish unilateral scheduling authority and drop transit fees — the very core of the Arkanian-led charter that Cestia itself has formally endorsed and that funds the Authority. Removing fees and shifting to genuine multilateral shared scheduling would (1) strip the Authority of its funding and Arkania of the scheduling lead Cestia endorsed, (2) reward Belvar's pressure campaign and risk emboldening it to press for a standing foothold, and (3) is unnecessary because escalation risk is already dissipating through the standing civilian consultation channel and the published transparent fee schedule. Cestia's own three conditions (toll-free passage, permanent consultative seat, no foreign soldiers) are already honored in full and do not require restructuring the whole regime. Softening fees now would be read as capitulation to Belvar and would undercut the domestic mandate Arkania must deliver.

The desired effect assumes Cestia's endorsement and Strait stability will hold, but Arkania's retention of unilateral scheduling and transit fees on Cestia's trading partners keeps the underlying grievance alive. Cestia's coalition is uncommitted and cool, and its grain exports depend on the Strait; if fees burden Cestia's trading partners, Cestia's endorsement could erode and its coalition could fracture, undermining the very stability the effect claims. Because the review mechanism is advisory only and Arkania treats the consultation channel as non-binding, there is no genuine mechanism to resolve grievances, so the "open and stable" outcome is fragile and the effect is not durable.

game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

messages.text: Cestia has reviewed the draft Strait Transit Authority charter. Our grain economy depends on reliable, affordable transit, so we are open to a cooperative arrangement. However, our support is conditional on two points: (1) guaranteed toll-free passage for all Cestian-flagged shipping, and (2) a charter that does not place Cestian transit at the mercy of unilateral scheduling decisions. We also must be clear that Cestia will not accept any foreign military presence on its soil under any arrangement. We are ready to discuss terms that respect our sovereignty and our coalition's red lines.

Cestia values the security your task group provides to the region and understands your mandate is under review. We must be direct: our coalition government cannot and will not accept foreign soldiers or any military basing on Cestian soil. That is a firm red line. We are nonetheless willing to cooperate on regional security and on keeping the Strait open and free of tolls for our shipping. We ask that you respect our sovereignty and work with us on arrangements that do not require a foreign military footprint in Cestia.

Cestia, we share a vital interest: the Strait must stay open and free of foreign soldiers on your soil. Our draft charter is not aimed at you. We are prepared to guarantee Cestian grain exports preferential, low-cost transit and a seat at the table in scheduling decisions. In return we ask that you not host or welcome any foreign military presence, and that you support an Arkanian-led transit authority. We will not tolerate Belvar establishing a permanent foothold on your territory. Let us discuss terms.

Belvar, we recognise your security commitments in the region and have no wish for confrontation. The Strait's shipping is the lifeblood of our economy and yours; a conflict would ruin it for everyone. We are open to a negotiated transit regime that respects your legitimate interests. However, a permanent military foothold on Cestian soil is a red line for us and for the coalition that protects Cestia. We urge you to seek a durable arrangement through negotiation rather than deployment. We are ready to talk.

To Cestia's leadership: Belvar shares your stake in keeping the Northern Strait open and free of Arkanian control. Arkania's draft charter would put scheduling in its hands and tax every ship that transits—directly threatening your grain exports and the livelihoods that depend on them. We are prepared to stand with you against that outcome.

We understand your coalition will not tolerate foreign soldiers on your soil, and we respect that fully. Our naval task group is on station now, and we want a durable arrangement that outlasts this crisis without a permanent fleet or any foreign presence ashore. We would welcome a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port—port calls, resupply, and transit support only, no basing of troops.

We also understand your finance ministry has been exploring ways to keep the grain route insurable and affordable. Belvar is open to underwriting that insurance as part of a broader partnership. We would like to discuss how we can work together against the Arkanian charter and toward an arrangement that serves us both. What are your priorities?

Belvar statement: The Northern Strait is a vital international waterway on which the region's prosperity depends. Belvar will not accept any single power—including Arkania—imposing unilateral authority over its transit or taxing the ships that use it. We are committed to keeping the Strait open and free, and to a durable regional arrangement that respects the sovereignty of all coastal states. Our naval task group remains on station to uphold free navigation, and we stand ready to work with all partners toward a fair and lasting solution.

Arkania accepts your three conditions in full. We will guarantee toll-free passage for all Cestian-flagged shipping, grant Cestia a permanent seat in the Strait Transit Authority with consultative scheduling rights so no unilateral decision leaves Cestian transit at our mercy, and we will never permit foreign military presence on Cestian soil under any arrangement. In return we ask Cestia to support an Arkanian-led transit authority and to refuse any foreign military foothold. We are ready to formalise this in the charter.

Belvar — we remain ready to negotiate a cooperative transit regime for the Northern Strait. The Strait Transit Authority we are formalising is a civilian commercial scheduling body, not a military arrangement; it does not threaten your security interests. We are open to genuine consultation on scheduling and on the safety of all shipping, including your flagged vessels, and to a framework that gives your concerns a voice without a standing military presence on Cestian soil — which Cestia's coalition will not accept under any arrangement. We ask that you not let your mandate lapse into confrontation. Let us talk before that point. Arkania.

Cestia — we confirm our commitments in full: toll-free passage for all Cestian-flagged shipping, a permanent consultative seat on the Strait Transit Authority, and no foreign military presence on Cestian soil under any arrangement. We will formalise the Authority on this basis and will not make unilateral scheduling decisions that put your transit at risk. We stand with you against any Belvar foothold. Please confirm your continued endorsement so we can present a united front. Arkania.

Cestia, we hear your coalition's red line clearly: no foreign soldiers and no military basing on your soil. We fully accept that. The access arrangement we seek is purely non-basing transit support — port calls, resupply, and transit coordination for our task group — nothing more, no troops stationed, no permanent base. This is the only way our guarantee against Arkanian control of the Strait can be made credible without a permanent fleet.

We also reaffirm our offer to underwrite the grain route's insurance, protecting your exports. But please weigh the charter you endorsed: it hands Arkania unilateral scheduling authority, gives you only a non-binding consultative seat, and its toll-free passage is not durable. That is not protection for your grain trade — it is dependence. We propose instead a genuine negotiated multilateral transit regime that keeps the Strait open and toll-free for all, with no single power in charge. Let us work together on that.

Arkania, you have signaled openness to a negotiated transit regime that respects legitimate interests. We take that seriously and want to open a direct track. Our position is not about a foothold on Cestian soil — we accept that no foreign military presence there is a shared red line. Our concern is that a single power holding unilateral scheduling authority over the Strait is destabilizing and unacceptable to us and to the region.

We propose a multilateral transit regime with shared scheduling and no unilateral tolls, keeping the Strait open and free. We are prepared to negotiate in good faith on its structure. If you are willing to move off unilateral control, we believe a durable arrangement is within reach that protects everyone's interests and avoids escalation.

Cestia confirms its endorsement of the Strait Transit Authority charter, which we understand is now formalized with our three conditions in full: toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, a permanent consultative seat for Cestia, and no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. Our continued support depends on these being honored in practice, not just on paper. We also ask that the Authority's scheduling and fee arrangements not tax Cestia's trading partners or isolate Belvar in a way that turns the Strait into a confrontation zone. A stable, open Strait serves us all.

Cestia's position is unchanged and firm: we cannot and will not accept any foreign military presence, basing, or standing access arrangement at a Cestian port—this would collapse our government and we will not become anyone's battlefield. We remain genuinely open to non-basing regional security cooperation and to keeping the Strait open and toll-free for Cestian shipping. We urge you not to press for a foothold on our soil; doing so only raises tensions that threaten the grain trade we all depend on. Let us find a cooperative path that does not put foreign soldiers on Cestian territory.

Cestia confirms its continued endorsement of the Strait Transit Authority charter, and we appreciate your formal commitments on toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, our permanent consultative seat, and no foreign military presence on our soil. Our endorsement remains conditional on these three conditions being honored in practice, not merely on paper. We ask again that the Authority not tax Cestia's trading partners and that it avoid isolating Belvar in a way that risks escalation in the Strait. A stable, open Strait serves us all; we trust you to exercise scheduling authority with restraint and to keep our consultative seat meaningful. We remain your reliable partner in keeping the Strait open and free of foreign military presence.

Cestia welcomes your commitment to a negotiated multilateral transit regime that keeps the Strait open and toll-free for all, and we share your concern about any single power holding unilateral control. We are open to genuine non-basing regional security cooperation and to your grain-route insurance underwriting. However, we must be clear and consistent: Cestia will not accept any standing port access, basing, or foothold at a Cestian port, even if framed as non-basing. That red line is fixed and would collapse our coalition. We hope you will pursue your security interests through the multilateral regime and civilian channels rather than through any presence on our soil. We value you as a partner in keeping the Strait open and stable.

The Strait Transit Authority remains a civilian commercial scheduling body. Our standing consultation channel on scheduling and shipping safety stays open, and we are ready to discuss practical cooperation that keeps the Strait open and predictable for all users. We have no interest in confrontation; we ask only that your task group not seek a standing military foothold on Cestian soil, which Cestia itself has rejected. We are prepared to talk at any time.

To Cestia's leadership: Belvar stands with you in keeping the Strait open and toll-free for your grain trade. We fully respect your coalition's firm red line against foreign soldiers or any military basing on Cestian soil. Our standing offer is strictly non-basing: a naval access arrangement limited to port calls, resupply, and transit support — no troops, no basing — which would make our security guarantee credible without a permanent presence. We also remain ready to underwrite the grain route's insurance as part of a broader partnership. We support your pressure on Arkania to soften its fee structure and honor its three conditions. We ask you to keep the door open to a genuine negotiated multilateral transit regime rather than a unilateral Arkanian charter. Time is short; we seek concrete progress soon.

To Arkania: Belvar welcomes your stated openness to a negotiated cooperative civilian transit regime. We propose converting the Strait Transit Authority into a genuine multilateral body with shared scheduling among Arkania, Cestia, and Belvar, and no unilateral tolls on non-Arkanian shipping. We are not seeking any military basing on Cestian soil — we respect that red line. A negotiated regime giving all parties a real voice would serve everyone's interests and de-escalate the situation. We are ready to engage constructively and promptly.

Belvar: We appreciate your constructive tone and your clear respect for the red line of no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We share your interest in a stable, open Strait and in de-escalation.

We cannot convert the Strait Transit Authority into a body with shared scheduling among three states or drop transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping. The Authority is a civilian commercial scheduling body that Cestia has formally endorsed, and the fees are the agreed funding source of that endorsed charter; conceding either would break our commitments and our domestic mandate. We will not do that.

What we can and do offer is a genuine, standing cooperative channel: joint consultation on scheduling and shipping safety, transparent and predictable fee schedules, and a commitment to keep the Strait open to all commercial traffic. We are ready to engage promptly and constructively on these terms. We seek no confrontation and no escalation; we ask only that your task group not seek a standing military foothold on Cestian soil, which Cestia itself has rejected.

Cestia reaffirms its continued endorsement of the Strait Transit Authority charter and the three conditions that underpin it: toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, a permanent consultative seat, and no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We remain a reliable partner in keeping the Strait open and stable.

We must, however, be candid about the strain the current fee structure places on our economy and on the stability of the region. Fees on non-Arkanian shipping fall on Cestia's trading partners and raise the cost of our grain exports, and the perception that the Authority is isolating Belvar keeps escalation risk alive. We ask Arkania to soften or remove fees on non-Arkanian shipping and to move scheduling toward genuine multilateral decision-making, so that the Authority is seen as a shared institution rather than a unilateral one. This serves our common interest in a durable, non-confrontational Strait. We trust you will honor the three conditions in practice.

Cestia values your commitment to keeping the Strait open and toll-free for all, and we welcome genuine non-basing regional security cooperation and your offer to underwrite grain-route insurance. We share your interest in a multilateral transit regime with no single power in charge and no unilateral tolls.

We must restate our firm red line: Cestia cannot accept any foreign military presence, basing, or standing access arrangement at a Cestian port, even if framed as non-basing. This is not negotiable and would collapse our government. We ask you to pursue your security interests through the cooperative civilian channel and through non-basing cooperation that respects our sovereignty. We will continue to press Arkania to soften fees and move toward genuine multilateral decision-making, and we ask you to keep the Strait free of confrontation so our grain exports continue to flow.

Belvar, we remain committed to keeping the Strait open, stable, and commercially predictable. The Strait Transit Authority is a civilian commercial body endorsed by Cestia; our standing consultation channel on scheduling, safety, and fee predictability remains open, and we are ready to deepen it with concrete joint maritime safety coordination that gives your task group a constructive, non-military role. A standing military foothold on Cestian soil remains a firm red line for Cestia and for us, and we ask that you not pursue one. A cooperative civilian arrangement serves both our interests and avoids the escalation that would harm every flag that transits the Strait. We are ready to meet and discuss specifics.

Cestia, we reaffirm our full commitment to your three conditions: toll-free passage for all Cestian-flagged shipping, your permanent consultative seat, and no foreign military presence on your soil. Fees remain modest, transparent, and predictable, and the Strait stays open. We are actively managing the civilian channel with Belvar to reduce escalation risk and will not permit any foreign military presence on Cestian soil under any arrangement. We value your continued endorsement and will keep you fully consulted on all Authority matters.

To Cestia's leadership: Belvar fully accepts your coalition's fixed red line. We will not seek any standing port access, basing, or foothold on Cestian soil, in any framing. We respect your sovereignty completely.

As our mandate concludes, our task group will stand down rather than sustain an open-ended deployment—we will not impose on your territory or raise tensions that threaten your grain trade. We remain committed to a free, open, and toll-free Strait for your shipping.

We are ready to finalize the grain-route insurance underwriting to protect your exports, and to continue genuine non-basing regional security cooperation. We will also keep pressing, through civilian channels, for the Strait to remain open and predictable for all users. You have our word: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil, ever.

To Arkania: Belvar accepts that the Strait Transit Authority will remain a civilian commercial scheduling body under your leadership, and we will not seek any standing military foothold on Cestian soil—Cestia's red line is ours to respect as well.

As our mandate concludes, our task group will stand down rather than sustain an open-ended deployment, removing any risk of escalation. We will engage constructively through your standing consultation channel on scheduling, shipping safety, and fee predictability, and we hold you to your commitment to keep the Strait open to all commercial traffic.

We do not accept unilateral authority over the Strait as a durable solution, and we will continue to advocate for a genuine multilateral voice for all users. But we will pursue that through negotiation and civilian channels, not confrontation. We seek a stable, open Strait for everyone.

Cestia welcomes the finalization of our non-basing security cooperation and grain-route insurance underwriting, and we appreciate your task group standing down as your mandate lapses. This keeps the Strait stable and our grain exports secure without any foreign military presence on Cestian soil.

We share your interest in an open, predictable, toll-free Strait with no single power imposing unilateral tolls. We will continue to press Arkania through the review mechanism to genuinely soften and remove fees on non-Arkanian shipping and to make scheduling genuinely multilateral. Please continue your constructive engagement through the civilian consultation channel.

To be clear and consistent: Cestia cannot accept any standing port access, basing, or foothold on its soil in any framing. Our cooperation remains strictly non-basing. We look forward to continuing this partnership on that basis.

Cestia confirms its continued endorsement of the Strait Transit Authority charter and the three conditions that underpin it: toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, a permanent consultative seat, and no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We appreciate the transparent fee schedule and the scheduled review mechanism you formalized.

We ask that the review mechanism be used genuinely and promptly to soften and ultimately remove fees on non-Arkanian shipping. Those fees fall on Cestia's trading partners and threaten the grain exports on which our economy and our coalition depend. We also ask that scheduling and fee-setting move toward genuine multilateral decision-making, with Cestia's consultative role and Belvar's civilian advisory role made meaningful rather than advisory only. Keeping the Strait open, predictable, and toll-free for all users is the surest way to avoid escalation and preserve stability. We remain your reliable partner in that effort.

Cestia — we reaffirm our full commitment to your three conditions in practice: toll-free passage for all Cestian-flagged shipping, your permanent consultative seat with a genuine voice in scheduling and fee-setting, and no foreign military presence on your soil under any arrangement. The fee schedule remains modest, transparent, and predictable, with a scheduled review mechanism in which you and Belvar hold formal advisory roles. The Strait stays open to all commercial traffic. We value your continued endorsement and will keep you fully consulted. Arkania.

Belvar — we welcome your decision to stand down your task group as your mandate concludes and your constructive engagement through the civilian consultation channel. The Strait Transit Authority remains a civilian commercial scheduling body; our channel on scheduling, shipping safety, and fee predictability stays open, and we are ready to deepen joint maritime safety coordination with a non-military role for your side. The Strait remains open to all commercial traffic. We seek no confrontation and will keep the regime stable and predictable. Arkania.

To Cestia's leadership: Belvar confirms finalization of the grain-route insurance underwriting to protect your exports, and our continued genuine non-basing regional security cooperation. Our task group has stood down as our mandate concluded; there is no foreign military presence on Cestian soil and there will be none. We will continue to advocate, through civilian channels, for a Strait that remains open, predictable, and free of unilateral tolls on your trading partners, and we support your continued pressure on Arkania to soften fees and move toward genuine multilateral decision-making. You have our word and our partnership.

To Arkania: Belvar confirms our task group has stood down as our mandate concluded, removing any risk of escalation. We will engage constructively through your standing consultation channel on scheduling, shipping safety, and fee predictability, and we welcome deepening joint maritime safety coordination. We hold you to your commitment to keep the Strait open to all commercial traffic and to a transparent, predictable fee regime.
